While the panel is folded the separator reads a value of zero.

path: a side panel with a heading that folds to a rail
tree.rule: SidePanel is the one side panel of a work screen: the sunken surface, neutral heading, dashed outside border with its overlapping fold button, the rail and the drag to resize or fold.

components.name: SiteFooter
components.job: The foot of a page of a website: a small logo, one line of text and a few links such as rules, privacy and Discord.
useWhen: A public page of a website ends with the same small line on every page.
A site needs a fixed place for its rules, its privacy page and its community links.

avoidWhen.case: The buttons at the foot of a form that save or cancel.
The band at the top of the site with the main links.

rules: Keep it small: a Logo at sm, one line in note and a few links; the main pages belong in SiteHeader.
Mark a link to another site external, so it opens a new tab.
Put it last in the page column, under the content, and give navigate the app router.
a11y: It is a footer landmark, and its links are a nav named by label.
An external link says it opens a new tab to a screen reader.

tree.rule: SiteFooter is the one line at the foot of a website page, under the app parts.

components.name: SiteHeader
components.job: The band at the top of every page of a website: the logo and the site title as the link home, the main links and the signed-in person.
useWhen: A website such as a store or a community site needs the same band on every page, signed in or not.
A page has no side nav and needs a few links to the main pages, such as Home, Browse and Rules.

avoidWhen.case: A desktop app draws the title bar of its own window.
The header belongs to one view or card inside the page.
The page needs a menu down the left with its own search.

rules: Pass brand with the logo, the site title, a label for the link and its href; the title hides on a very narrow screen.
Pass links only for a page with no side nav, and activeId for the page shown; under 640 px they fold into one menu button.
Pass profile, a WindowTitleBar dropdown action, for the signed-in person: the same action object works in an app title bar.
Signed out, leave profile out and put a Sign in Button in actions.
Build the rest of the page from the app parts: SideNavLayout for the left menu, SettingsPage for a page, Card, FilterBar and DataTable.
Give navigate the app router so a link changes the page without a reload.
a11y: It is a header landmark; the logo and the title are one link home named by brand.label.
The links are a nav named by label, with aria-current on the page shown.
The phone menu and the profile are menu buttons with aria-haspopup, and their menus take the keys of DropdownMenu.

tree.rule: SiteHeader is the one site-only part on top of the page; everything under it is an app part.

components.name: Splash
components.job: The splash of the static page drawn from React, so the app can show it again, or take over from the static page with no jump.
useWhen: The app has loaded and has to wait again for the whole window, such as a lost engine it reconnects to or an update that restarts it.
The app takes over from a static splash page and keeps showing the splash until its own start tasks finish.

avoidWhen.case: One part of the page failed and the rest still works.
Work inside a page the user can still use.
A long job the user can hide or cancel.

rules: Before the bundle loads, write the same page in static HTML with splash.css; give both the same title, mark, status and version, so the hand-over shows no change.
Keep status to one short line that says what runs now; put a readable reason for a failure in detail and the raw error in error, which waits behind Details.

Pass a BrandMark or Logo as mark and it takes its dark ground look by itself; an image URL points at brand/dark-ground/<app>.svg or a mark PNG beside it, and an app mark of its own keeps its edge at 3:1 on the gradient, every shape or an outline around them.

Pass wordmark, an image URL such as brand/<app>-wordmark.svg, to show the app wordmark in place of the title text; on the static page put an img of class ts-wordmark inside ts-title, with the title as its alt.
The wordmark keeps its own size up to 48 px high and 384 px wide, keeping its proportions, so a wide one takes less height; draw it at least 48 px high.

For a pixel art wordmark, a small sprite, set wordmarkPixelated and add ts-wordmark--pixelated on the static img: it scales up to the 384 px row with hard pixel edges; auto decides once the picture loads, as on Image.
It sits on the dark gradient of the palette; an app theme that changes the palette seeds sets --p-gradient-dark-from and --p-gradient-dark-to too, dark enough that the text stays at WCAG AA.
Pass progress as a fraction from 0 to 1 when the steps are known, and indeterminate when they are not.
Show actions only when the user has something to do, such as Retry and Report a bug after a failure; mark Retry primary.
It covers the window; while it covers a mounted app, set inert on the app root so keys do not reach it.
a11y: The title is the h1 of the splash, and the status line is a polite live region, so each new step is read out.
With wordmark the h1 holds the image, and title becomes its alt text, so the heading keeps the app name.
When failed turns on, the status line becomes an alert and focus moves to the first primary action.
The bar is a progressbar named by progressLabel, Loading by default, with its value in percent.
The mark is decoration and hidden from screen readers.

path: the app is starting, or starting again
tree.rule: Splash draws the classes of splash.css, so it looks the same as the static splash page.

components.name: StageScreen
components.job: One big open stage for custom work with no navigation of its own, under the page header, which holds an optional toolbar and a Done button.
useWhen: Controller calibration, HUD layout, a map or an editor the app draws itself.
The content is one surface, not pages or sections.

avoidWhen.case: The screen has pages the user moves between.
The screen is read, such as About or credits.
The app runs one short task and reports a status.

rules: Give it an icon and a heading for the page header, which StageScreen always shows and nothing turns off.
Keep the toolbar to a status and a few tools; it sits in the header after the heading and is not a place for navigation.
Short of room, the toolbar moves to a row under the heading and wraps its items, while Done stays beside the heading.
Lay out the stage with intrinsic sizes, such as minmax(min(100%, 384px), 1fr) columns, so it fits a narrow window without sideways scroll.
Set done when the work ends with a clear finish; the close button still closes without it.
Put each calibration step on the stage in its own Card, with a SectionHeader that says what to do.
The stage scrolls when its content is larger; a canvas that pans itself sets its own size to fill the stage.
a11y: The card is a modal dialog named by the title.
Custom content on the stage brings its own roles and keyboard support.

path: one big custom surface, such as calibration
tree.rule: One open stage with an optional toolbar.

components.name: StatTile
components.job: A small tile with one headline number: its name, the value with a unit, how it moved, and an optional chart.
useWhen: A dashboard or a widget shows a few key readings, each with its change since the last one.
A reading needs its trend drawn beside it, such as frame rate with a Sparkline.

avoidWhen.case: A plain label and value on one line, with no trend or chart.
One value against its limit, as a round meter.

rules: Set trend from the change, and upIs from what a rise means: good for frame rate, bad for frame time.
Keep delta short, such as +4 or -2.1, and leave the unit to the unit prop.
Pass a Sparkline as chart, below the value in a narrow tile and beside it in a wide one.
Use tone on the value only when the reading is past its limit.
Pick size md for a widget grid, sm for a dense one and lg for a reading that leads a page.
a11y: The trend arrow is named Rising, Falling or Steady, so a screen reader hears the direction with the delta.
The label, value and unit are plain text read in order; the chart speaks only when it has a label.

path: a headline number with its trend
tree.rule: StatTile puts one reading, its change and its trend together in a tile sized for a widget grid.

components.name: StatusBar
components.job: The thin bar at the foot of an editor window: a row of labelled readouts such as cursor, zoom, colour and frame.
useWhen: An editor or tool window shows live facts about its work, such as the pixel under the pointer and the current zoom.
A readout needs a small colour chip beside its value, such as the colour you are drawing with.

avoidWhen.case: The save state of a form and its Save and Discard buttons.
One label and value on a line inside a panel, not a bar.
A headline number with its trend and chart.

rules: Give each item a stable id, a short label and a value; keep the value short, such as 24, 17 or 800%.
Set align to end for the readouts that describe the document, such as layer and frame, and leave the rest at the start.
Set priority from 1 to 3 on the readouts that may go when the bar is narrow: 3 goes first, 1 last. An item with no priority never goes.
Pass swatch as a CSS colour value and put the colour name or hex in the value, so the chip is never the only signal.
Use tone on a value only when it is past a limit, and title for a longer description on hover.
Pass actions for the few buttons that belong to the bar, such as sync or export; they end the bar as icon buttons with a tooltip.
Give the bar a label that names the region, such as Editor status.
Pass onItemContextMenu to open the app menu of a readout. It gets the item id and the event, from a right click, the Menu key or Shift+F10.
a11y: The bar is a labelled region and each readout is a term and its value in a description list.
It has no live region, so a cursor position that changes on every pointer move is never announced.
To announce a change, such as a finished export, use a separate live region, not the bar.
Each action is a button named by its label, shown as a tooltip too; loading marks it busy and disabled takes it out of the Tab order.
The swatch is hidden from assistive technology; its colour is read from the value beside it.
With onItemContextMenu each readout is a tab stop with a focus ring, so the Menu key and Shift+F10 reach it.

path: the status line at the foot
tree.rule: StatusBar is the one thin line of readouts at the foot of an editor window.

components.name: StudioLayout
components.job: The frame of a studio screen: a list on the left, an editor in the centre and an inspector on the right, under an optional bar of actions.
useWhen: A screen edits one thing picked from a list, with its properties beside it, such as a sprite, a language or a song studio.
The editor needs tools on its top edge and the screen needs Save and Export actions above it.
The user folds the side panels away now and then to give the editor the room.

avoidWhen.case: A list sits beside the detail of the picked item, with no inspector.
The user moves panels around and docks them.
Only one side panel sits beside the main view.

rules: Pass the editor as children and name it with editorLabel; it sits in a ToolFrame that scrolls.
Pass toolbar as ToolGroups groups, { id, label, content }, for the tools on the top edge of the editor.
Pass compactToolbar to keep that toolbar to one row of small controls with the group names hidden, when every row of height counts.
Pass start and end as { title, content } with any SidePanel prop, such as storageKey, width, actions, rail or defaultCollapsed; every panel resizes and folds by drag.
Pass bar as { title, caption, status, groups, idleHint } for the raised top bar; its HintLine shows the hint of the control under the pointer.
Put status and error lines in bar.notices, under the hint line, and a full width line, such as where an installed item came from, in banner.
Give the buttons in the bar and the toolbar a hint, { label, description }: the layout is one HintScope.
Give the layout a height, such as the window or a flex parent; the panels and the editor scroll inside it.
The columns stack, list, editor, then inspector, only when the open panels, the folded rails and the editor do not fit side by side; the body then scrolls.
Pass editorMinWidth for the narrowest editor the screen can work with, 192 px when left out; fold a panel to keep the columns on a narrow window.
a11y: The bar is a header with the title as a heading, h1 unless bar.level says otherwise.
Each side panel is an aside named by its title, with a heading; the editor is a section named by editorLabel.
The fold buttons are CollapseToggles: they say Hide or Show and the title, report aria-expanded and keep focus when the panel folds.
Each group in the bar and the toolbar is a group named by its label, shown above it unless compactToolbar hides it.

path: a list, an editor and an inspector side by side
tree.rule: StudioLayout draws every studio screen the same way: a raised bar, two SidePanels and a ToolFrame for the editor.

components.name: TaskProgress
components.job: The progress of one long job: a bar, the current line, its steps, the error when it fails and its log, folded.
useWhen: A job runs for seconds or minutes, such as a generation, an engine setup or a download, and the user waits on it.
The job has named steps, writes output lines, or can fail with a message the user must read.

avoidWhen.case: The job should sit in a dialog the user can hide or cancel.
Only a bar is needed, with no line, steps or log.
The user walks through the steps and picks when to go on.

rules: Pass percent only when the job knows it; leave it out and the running bar sweeps.
Write the line as what happens now, such as Downloading Python: 31 of 84 MB, and update it as the job moves.
Pass the error as a sentence that says what failed and what to do; it shows once the state is failed.
Keep every output line in log, so the user can read why a job failed.
a11y: The section is named by label, and the bar by the same name.
The state word is a status region, so a screen reader hears Done, Failed or Cancelled when it changes.
The error is an alert, and the log sits behind a Disclosure that says whether it is open.

path: a long job with steps, a log or a failure
tree.rule: TaskProgress draws a bar, the steps, the failure and the log of one job the same way in every app.

components.name: Toast
components.job: A short message in a corner of the window that leaves on its own, raised with toast() from any part of the app and drawn by the one ToastStack.
useWhen: Something finished or failed out of view, such as a save written or a sync lost, and the user should hear of it once.
A failure can be tried again from the message itself, with an action such as Retry.

avoidWhen.case: The note must stay on the page until the user acts.
The user must answer before the app goes on.

rules: Mount one ToastStack at the root of the app and raise every toast with toast(); never draw a stack of your own.
Keep the message to one short sentence that says what happened, such as Save state written to slot 3.
Raise the same message again, not a new one: it joins the toast on screen and shows a count.
Pass an id when the text changes but it is the same event, such as a sync count, so it still joins one toast.
Set duration to 0 only when the toast carries an action the user must see.
Pass onClose to follow the life of the toast, such as a delete that runs unless Undo was pressed: it runs once, with expired, dismissed, action or replaced.
Raise each undo toast with its own id when deletes can follow each other: a toast that joins the same message closes the one before with replaced.
Pass undo in place of action for an Undo, such as after a load: Ctrl+Z runs it too while the toast shows, through the one stack of useUndo.
a11y: The stack is a polite status region, so a screen reader reads each toast once.
A danger toast is an alert and is read at once.
A toast waits while the pointer or focus is on it, then starts its full time again, and gives focus back when it leaves.

tree.rule: Toast keeps one queue per app: every part raises through toast(), the stack caps how many show and the same message shows once with a count.

components.name: Toolbar
components.job: A row or a column of tools, built from data, with a hint on each, a menu beside the tools that have options, and More for the tools that do not fit.
useWhen: An editor has a rail of tools the user picks from, such as pencil, eraser and fill, along an edge of the work area.
A tool has options, such as a brush size, that should open beside it on hover without a dialog.
The same tools must work in a row and in a column, and fold the ones that do not fit.
A wide panel lists the same tools as rows with their name, description and shortcut.

avoidWhen.case: The buttons are the actions of one item and fold into More when narrow.
The user picks one value for a form field from a short list.
The actions are rare or secondary and one button can hold them all.

rules: Keep every value in the app; the toolbar draws items and calls onSelect, onChange and the options of each item.
An item is a button, a toggle, a group of choices, a number or a separator. A tool the user picks is a toggle with pressed set on the current one.
orientation horizontal shows the optional caption beside the icon; vertical shows icons only. The hint always carries the name, the description and the shortcut.
labels false hides the caption in a horizontal bar, so it shows icons only. It defaults to true. A ToolbarDock passes its value for the toolbar in the render slot.
icon is a name from the set or any node, such as your own bitmap. A name keeps its icon size and the 24 px snap of a pixel icon; a node is drawn as given, in the button and in More.

Give shortcut as text such as Ctrl+Z, as keys, or as a list of { label, keys } such as Smaller and Larger. The hint draws one Shortcut row for each; the folded menu keeps the first. It never sits on the button.

options on a button or toggle are DropdownMenu groups. They open on hover below a row and beside a column, and with the arrow key that points away from the toolbar. openOn click opens them on a press instead, and the press still runs onSelect or onChange.

menuSide right or left says which side of a vertical toolbar its menus open on; a ToolbarDock slot hands it over, so a left bar opens right and a right bar opens left. Menus flip and stay inside the view near any edge, and look the same on every side.

layout list draws each item as a row with its icon, name, description and shortcut, a group as a labelled set of rows and a number as a row with its field. Use it in a wide panel; it never folds and has no handle or caption.
Items that do not fit fold into More, in order; a group becomes a labelled set of choices and a number becomes a slider.
handle draws a grip at the start. A dock wires its own pointer handlers through handleProps; the toolbar has no drag logic.
Give the toolbar a length: a row takes the width of its parent and a column the height of its parent. Without one, nothing folds.
a11y: The toolbar has role toolbar, aria-orientation and a name from label. Only one item is a tab stop.
Arrow Right and Left in a row, or Down and Up in a column or a list, move focus and wrap; Home and End go to the ends.
The arrow key that points away from the toolbar opens the options of the focused tool and moves focus into the menu. Escape closes it and returns focus to the tool.
In a number field the arrow keys edit the value; Escape moves focus back to the item before it.
A toggle reports aria-pressed and a tool with options reports aria-haspopup and aria-expanded. The shortcut is set as aria-keyshortcuts.

path: tools in a row or column, with hints and options
tree.rule: Toolbar is the set of tools of an editor, with a hint on each and options beside the ones that have them.

components.name: ToolbarDock
components.job: The frame around a work area that holds toolbars on its four edges, up to two lanes on each, with the work area in the centre.
useWhen: An editor has several toolbars that sit along the edges of the work area, such as tools on the left and options on top.
The toolbars are described by data, and each one has a side it belongs to by default.
The work area is a WidgetManager or a DockLayout that should take the room the toolbars leave.

avoidWhen.case: One row or column of tools needs no edge frame around the work area.
The panels around the work area are widgets that tile, float and tab.
A single toolbar sits on the top edge of one frame.

rules: layout says which toolbar sits on which side. The dock draws it and never stores it; the app keeps it and saves it.
Top and bottom lanes span the full width. Left and right lanes sit between them, so the corners belong to top and bottom.
A side holds at most MAX_LANES lanes, which is two. MAX_PER_SIDE is a deprecated alias of it. The first lane of a side is the outer lane, the one next to the window edge.

layout.sides[side] is a list of lanes, and a lane is a list of places { id, start, size }. start and size are fractions of the lane, from 0 to 1, so a lane can hold several toolbars with gaps between them. layout.corners says which side claims each corner. Read the ids of a side with toolbarIdsOf(layout, side), never by indexing sides.
migrateToolbarLayout(saved, definitions) reads a saved layout of any version, upgrades a v1 layout to v2 and cleans a v2 one. Pass every saved layout through it.
definitions names each toolbar. A toolbar in the layout without a definition is not drawn, and a hidden toolbar is not drawn.
renderToolbar draws one toolbar and gets its orientation, its side, menuSide, the handle and labels. Pass the orientation, menuSide, the handle and labels to Toolbar.

layout.labels is optional and maps a toolbar id to true or false. Missing means the default of the app, and the slot then has no labels. setToolbarLabels(layout, id, on) sets it and returns the same layout when nothing changes. The layout version stays 2, and migrateToolbarLayout keeps valid entries and drops the rest.

moveToolbarToSide(layout, id, side) moves a shown toolbar to a side, placed as showToolbar places it: its last spot on that side if free, else a new lane, else the largest gap. With no room, or when the toolbar is already on that side, it returns the same layout. last is kept as it was.
The orientation comes from the side: horizontal on top and bottom, vertical on left and right. It is never stored.
The handle is the set of props for the grip of a Toolbar. It carries the toolbar id as data-drag-toolbar and a name such as Move Drawing tools.
Dragging the grip moves the toolbar. A preview shows the lane it will take, with the thickness of that side, so the switch between horizontal and vertical shows before the drop.

The drop lands where the pointer is along the lane, snapped to the lane ends and to the ends of its neighbours within 8 px. The bar keeps its last size, shrunk to the room left and never below MIN_BAR_PX, and the neighbours shift along as they do for an end handle. A drop with no room is refused, and so is a third lane. The centre is never a target.
Drop on the basket at the bottom of the frame to hide the toolbar. Escape, or a drop anywhere else, puts it back.
The keyboard does the same without a pointer. Enter or Space on the grip picks the toolbar up and opens the move guide, which lists the keys.

While picked up, an arrow key goes to that side, to a new outer lane first. The same arrow again steps to a new inner lane, then to each lane already there. PageUp and PageDown step through the slots of the lane: its start, between its bars, its end. Home and End go to the first and last slot.
Delete sends the picked toolbar to the basket. Enter drops it and Escape puts it back. The preview shows the target as it does for a pointer drag.

Each toolbar has a thin handle at both ends, shown on hover or focus. Dragging one moves that end along the lane. A neighbour in the way is pushed along with its size kept, and the chain stops at the lane ends. A bar never gets shorter than MIN_BAR_PX.
The end handles are separators. Arrow keys move the end by 8 px, Shift by 64 px, Home and End go to the ends of its range. The result is announced, with the toolbars it pushed.

Dragging the first start handle of a lane below 0, or the last end handle past the lane end, takes the corner: each lane of the other side whose half thickness is passed gives it up, and the bars of the yielding lanes keep their pixel position and are pushed along. If they cannot fit, the take stops. Dragging back gives the corner back. At the lane end, one more outward arrow takes the next corner lane and an inward arrow gives it back. The pure op is takeToolbarCorner(origin, metrics, grip, px), and metrics needs laneThickness.

The pure ops are resizeToolbarEnd(origin, metrics, id, end, px), always computed from the layout at the start of the gesture, and toolbarEndRange(layout, metrics, id, end) for the value, min and max of a handle in pixels along the lane.

onLayoutChange gets the new layout when a drag or a keyboard move ends. It is not called when the toolbar is dropped where it already was. The dock never changes the layout by itself, so keep it in state.

useToolbarLayout({ value, onChange, definitions }) wraps the pure ops for a controlled layout. It gives move, show, hide, toggle, isShown, canShow and reset, and calls onChange once per edit, never when the edit changes nothing.

toolbarMenuGroups(definitions, layout, toggle, menu) gives DropdownMenu groups for a Toolbars menu: a check item per toolbar, checked when shown and disabled when its side has no free lane, plus a Reset toolbars item when menu.onReset is set. menu is the toolbars group of useTesseraStrings with onReset added.
children fills the centre cell and takes the room the lanes leave. Give the dock a height, as the centre has none of its own.
a11y: Each toolbar keeps its own role toolbar, orientation and name from the Toolbar you render.
The grip is a button named Move followed by the label of the toolbar from definitions.
Focus returns to the grip when a drag or a keyboard move ends or is cancelled.
Every keyboard step is announced in a polite live region, for example Drawing tools: left, outer lane. The slot, a spot with no room and the drop are announced too.

path: toolbars the user docks on the edges of a work area
tree.rule: ToolbarDock is the frame that holds the toolbars on the edges of a work area, up to two lanes on each side.

components.name: TrackTable
components.job: A flat, read-only table whose columns share the width in fractions and drop out, least needed first, as the table narrows.
useWhen: A few rows with a few cells each, such as the agents of a node, sit on a page or inside a card with no frame of their own.
The table lives in a pane or a drawer whose width changes, and the least needed columns may leave when it is narrow.

avoidWhen.case: The user sorts, groups, resizes or selects among many records.
The user edits the rows in place.
Each row is a label and a value, with no columns to compare.

rules: Give each column a fr, its share of the width; leave it out for 1.
Mark a column drop 1, 2 or 3 to hide it below 768, 640 or 480 px of table width; 1 leaves first.
Never mark the column that names the row: it stays at every width.
Draw state with Status and groups with Tag inside cell; the table sets no look for them.
Put the table in a Card when it needs a frame; it draws no border or background.
Pass empty for the message shown when there are no rows.
a11y: The table is named by label, and each cell is read in its row; a dropped column is removed from the reading order too.
Give a column whose label would be a symbol a text label, since the header is the only name of its cells.

path: a flat table of rows that drops columns as it narrows
tree.rule: TrackTable shares the width by fractions and drops the least needed columns by the width of the table, not the window.

components.name: UtilityScreen
components.job: A compact screen for one short task, laid out as the rotp update dialog: the window header shows the status with a spinner or a tone icon and the close button, then one column with a centred message, settings, details, a framed notes box and progress, then a report button over a rule and the actions.
useWhen: The app checks for updates, imports a file or tests a connection, and shows how it went.
The task has a few states, each with its own title, message and actions.

avoidWhen.case: The user answers one question and nothing runs.
The screen holds settings or several pages.
The screen is read, such as About or credits.
The screen is one big custom surface.

rules: The status is the header at the top of the window, with the close button at its end: status.title is its title and names the window, and the tone picks its icon. There is no card inside the window.
Set status.tone to busy while the task runs; it shows a spinner in place of the icon. Use status.icon for a closer icon, such as a download arrow.
Write the status title as the state, such as Update available, and the message as one short line, such as the version.
When the task fails, pass the raw error in status.error: it waits behind Details under the message.
Mark the action that tries a failed task again with retry, so it shows as a RetryButton with the label of the action.
Put choices that shape the task, such as a pre-release toggle or a version picker, in settings, not in the children.
Put long text, such as release notes, in notes: a framed box with its own scroll. Draw a release note with Markdown, size sm, headingOffset 2 and hideTitle, since the box title names the version.
Set progress only when the task can say how far it is.
Pass report to offer a way to report a problem: one red bug icon button over a rule, with report.footnote as a short line beside it.
Put the main action last in actions, with tone primary, and keep one primary action.
In a narrow or short window the card fills the room: the body scrolls, and the footer with the actions stays in view.
a11y: The status title and the message are live regions: a screen reader reads each new one.
The report button is named Report an issue from the strings, and shows the same words in a tooltip.
The card is a modal dialog named by the status title.

path: one short task with a status, such as an update check
tree.rule: A status, details and actions in a compact window.

components.name: ValidationSummary
components.job: What blocks a save, listed above the form in a toned box, each problem a link that moves focus to its field.
useWhen: A form or an editor cannot save or run until the user fixes one or more fields.
The problems sit in fields the user may not see, such as rows of a long list or another section.

avoidWhen.case: One note with no list, such as a warning about the whole page.
Only one field is wrong and it is in view; its own error is enough.
A step of a wizard reports what stops it going on.

rules: Write each problem as what to fix, such as Enter the path of the key file, and give it the field it belongs to.
Move focus to the field in onFocusField, and scroll it into view; the summary does not know the form.
Keep tone danger for what blocks the save, and warning for options to check that do not.
Show the summary once the user tries to save, or keep it in step with the form; leave it out when nothing is wrong.
a11y: The box is an alert, so a screen reader reads the title and the problems when it appears.
The problems are a list; one with a field is a button named by its message, the arrow hidden.
And N more shows the rest and moves focus to the first problem it revealed.

path: what blocks a save, with a jump to each field
tree.rule: ValidationSummary lists what blocks a save in one place and takes the user to each field, the same way in every editor.

components.name: Video
components.job: A video player with its own control bar: seek with a time preview, volume, speed, picture in picture, theater mode and full screen.
useWhen: A replay, a clip or a live stream plays inside the app.
The user seeks, changes the volume or the speed, or watches in full screen.

avoidWhen.case: A still picture holds its box, such as a poster or a screenshot.
A small framed preview stands for the video in a list, as an Image with frame.

rules: Give it a label that names the video, such as Boss fight replay; the player is a group named by it.
Size the player through its class with an aspect ratio, since the bar sits over the bottom of the video.
Let the page own theater mode through theater and onTheaterChange when the layout around the player changes with it.
Set controls to false for a background or a preview with no bar.
A video that fails to load shows errorMessage over the player with a Retry that loads the source again; with controls off, the Retry is left out.
a11y: The player takes focus: Space or K plays and pauses, the arrows skip five seconds, M mutes, F goes full screen and T sets theater mode.
The seek bar reads the time as 1:05 of 3:20, and Page Up, Page Down, Home and End jump along it.
The speed menu holds radio items: the arrows move, Enter picks, Escape closes it and focus goes back to its button.
The bar fades while the video plays and the pointer rests, and comes back on a key, a move or focus.

tree.rule: Video draws its bar over the video in white on black in every theme, and keeps its speed menu and volume inside the frame so they work in full screen.

components.name: VirtualGrid
components.job: A very long grid of equal tiles, such as sprite thumbnails, in sections if wanted, where only the rows in view are drawn, with the arrow keys to move between tiles.
useWhen: The grid has thousands of tiles, such as every frame of a sprite sheet or every image of a folder, and drawing them all would slow the page.
Every tile is the same size and the app draws the content of each tile.
The tiles fall into groups, such as the folders of a library, each under a header row that collapses.
The user moves through the tiles with the keys and the grid must scroll to follow.

avoidWhen.case: A long list of rows, one per line.
A short set of cards that can all be drawn at once.
Records with columns the user sorts, groups or resizes.

rules: Give it items, getKey and renderItem; getKey returns a stable id, never the position.
Give label a name for the grid, since the tiles are drawn without a heading of their own.
Size the grid from its parent: it fills the height of its box and scrolls inside it.

Pick a square tile with tileSize, the name of a size token such as size-96; tileWidth and tileHeight size a tile that is not square and win over tileSize; the columns that fit the width of the box are worked out from the width, and a raw pixel number is not accepted.
Give sections instead of items to group the tiles: each section has a key, a label and its items, and an optional count to show in the header instead of the number of items.
The index given to renderItem, getKey and onActiveChange runs through all the sections, and onActiveChange is not called for a header.
A header spans all the columns and takes part in the scroll like a row of its own; its height is fixed by the grid.

A section takes actions, the same list of actions as an ItemCard, drawn as icon buttons at the end of its header, and depth, a whole number that indents the header by one step per level for nested folders.
Hold the collapsed sections with collapsed (a list of keys) and onToggleSection(key, collapsed), or leave both out and give defaultCollapsed for the start; keep the list stable between renders.

Give scrollRef the ref of a marquee container and spread bind of useMarqueeSelect on the grid; every tile carries data-marquee-key set to its getKey, and overlay takes the MarqueeBox that follows the content.

Give ref a ref and call scrollToIndex(index, align) to scroll a tile into view; align is start, center, end or nearest, and nearest is the default; the index of a tile in a collapsed section scrolls to its header.

Give a marquee every tile, drawn or not, with getRects on the ref: useMarqueeSelect({ getRects: () => gridRef.current?.getRects() ?? [] }); the rects come from the layout, not the page, and the tiles of a collapsed section are left out.

Give renderTile instead of renderItem when a tile is a button or a card with an action: it receives (item, index, cell) and the app spreads cell on the tile, so the tile is the gridcell and the only focus target; a cell with a button inside is two targets, and the smaller inner one fails the target size check.

The cell props carry the role, tabIndex, aria-colindex, the data attributes the keys and the marquee read, the focus and key handlers, and a className that removes the padding; keep that className when you add your own, and spread them on one element that can take focus.
Give renderTile or renderItem, not both; renderItem stays the default for tiles that are not interactive, and the grid wraps them in a padded cell as before.
Keep renderItem cheap and free of its own size; the tile cuts what does not fit, and the tile pads its content.
Raise overscan for tiles that load slowly while the user scrolls fast; the default is 2 rows on each side.
Use onActiveChange to follow the tile that holds focus, such as to show its detail beside the grid.
a11y: The grid is a grid of cells with the row and column of each, so a reader hears where the tile is among thousands.

One tile is in the tab order; the four arrows move by a tile or a row, Home and End go to the start or end of the row, Ctrl with them goes to the first or last tile, and Page Up and Page Down move by a screen of rows.
A header is a cell that says if it is open; Enter, Space and a click toggle it, Left closes it and Right opens it, and Right on an open header goes to its first tile.
Up and Down move between the tiles and the headers, and Left and Right step through tiles to the next header and back.
A tile or a header that holds focus stays drawn when it scrolls out of view, so the keys keep working.
The actions of a header are in the tab order after the header; the arrows, Enter, Space, Left and Right act only when the header itself has focus, and a click on an action does not toggle the header.
Keys act only when the tile itself has focus, so a field inside a tile keeps its own arrow keys.
With renderTile the tile is the cell, so a reader meets one control per tile; Enter and Space still press a button tile, and the arrows move between tiles.

path: a long grid of equal tiles drawn only where it is in view
tree.rule: VirtualGrid draws only the rows of tiles in view, so a grid of any size opens at once and scrolls smoothly.

components.name: VirtualList
components.job: A very long list of rows of one height, where only the rows in view are drawn, with the arrow keys to move between them.
useWhen: The list has thousands of items, such as a log of events or every file of a folder, and drawing them all would slow the page.
Every row is the same height and the app draws the content of each row.
The user moves through the rows with the keys and the list must scroll to follow.

avoidWhen.case: Records with columns the user sorts, groups or resizes.
A short list where every row can be drawn at once.
Files with their size, date and open buttons.

rules: Give it items, getKey and renderItem; getKey returns a stable id, never the position.
Give label a name for the list, since the rows are drawn without a heading of their own.
Size the list from its parent: it fills the height of its box and scrolls inside it.
Pick rowSize compact, normal or roomy; the height comes from a token and is measured once from the first row, so keep every row the same height.
For a height of your own pass rowHeight, the name of a size token such as size-64; it wins over rowSize, and a raw pixel number is not accepted.
Keep renderItem cheap and free of its own height; the row cuts what does not fit.
Raise overscan for rows that load slowly while the user scrolls fast; the default is 10 rows on each side.
Use onActiveChange to follow the row that holds focus, such as to show its detail beside the list.
a11y: The list is a list of items, each with its position and the size of the list, so a reader hears 41 of 5000.
One row is in the tab order; the arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down move focus and scroll to it.
A row that holds focus stays drawn when it scrolls out of view, so the keys keep working.
Keys act only when the row itself has focus, so a field inside a row keeps its own arrow keys.

path: a long list drawn only where it is in view
tree.rule: VirtualList draws only the rows in view, so a list of any length opens at once and scrolls smoothly.

components.name: Widget
components.job: The frame of a tool panel, such as a player list or a log, that the user docks, floats or pops out; WidgetManager places a whole dock.
useWhen: An app shows several tool panels around its main view and lets the user arrange them, as a dashboard of a session.
Some panels only make sense in a context, such as a running session or a race, and step aside outside it.

avoidWhen.case: Two fixed panes share the space and the user only moves the line between them.
One panel slides in from the edge for a moment.

rules: Draw a dock with WidgetManager and keep the layout in the app: it hands every change to onLayoutChange.
Answer contextActive with one flag, or with a function that reads each definition, such as its own context field.
Keep that function stable with useCallback; Tessera calls it only for the widgets shown in context only.
Give a log or a chart fill in its definition, and leave the other widgets on the default padding.
Give every widget of a kit, such as developer tools, the same group: it then never tabs or splits with a widget outside it.
A widget in its own window takes disabled, with the reason as a string, so it shows the state WidgetManager draws when docked.
Give a definition dockWeight to size it on an edge: weight 2 takes twice the room of 1, and none counts as 1.
Give a definition an icon to draw it before the title or tab label; it is decorative, as the label names the widget.
Give a button in titleBarActions or widgetActions size xs, the 20 px of the built-in title bar buttons.
Give the widgets of a kit chrome compact or none in their definition, and pass the same chrome to a Widget in its own window.
To tell the options panel and its sub-panels, such as Shortcuts, from other menus, match the WIDGET_OPTIONS_ATTRIBUTE attribute with closest.
a11y: Each widget is a region named by its title, or by its open tab in a tabbed pane; pop out, options and close are icon buttons named with it.
Each widget carries data-widget-id and each pane data-pane-id, for tests.
A hidden context only widget leaves the tree, so focus never lands in a panel that is not shown.
A disabled widget keeps its frame working; its body is inert and marked aria-disabled, with the reason over it.
With chrome none the buttons stay in the tab order and the tree; focus inside the widget shows them, and the title still names it.

path: panels the user docks and moves
tree.rule: Widget and WidgetManager give every tool panel the same frame, dock and options, with the app holding the layout.

components.name: WindowTitleBar
components.job: The title bar of a frameless desktop window: the brand in the middle, the main menu at the start and the window buttons at the end.
useWhen: A desktop app draws its own window frame and needs a title bar that drags the window and holds its buttons.
A few app wide actions earn a place beside the brand, such as Search, Report a bug, or a menu of window groups.

avoidWhen.case: The header belongs to one view inside the window, with its own title and actions.
The window is a page or a dialog of the app, not the frame of the app itself.

rules: The app owns the window state: pass maximized, fullscreen and pinned, and act on each control in onControl.
Hide a control the host lacks in controls, such as close: false; controls={false} hides them all, for a host with no window buttons.
Every action but a volume has a label and an icon; tone and effect mark the icon, the same on a command, a status or a dropdown action.
Set disabled on an action that cannot run now, such as Undo with nothing to undo; disabledReason says why in its tooltip.
Use bar volume for a sound level: the bar draws VolumeControl, and the main menu lists a Mute or Unmute row and a slider row named by label.
Use bar dropdown for an action with a few choices of its own; narrow windows fold it into the main menu as a sub-menu.
Keep the actions few: narrow windows move them into the main menu, then shrink the brand.
The main menu hamburger turns into an X while its menu is open; no other menu button in Tessera does.
view moves the View sub-menu to a group and position of menu; view={false} hides it, and the main menu then lists pin and full screen while the bar tucks them away.
viewItems adds your own entries to the View sub-menu, after the pin and full screen rows and a separator; they are DropdownMenu nodes, so check items and sub-menus work.
With view={false} and viewItems set, the main menu still draws a View sub-menu holding only the viewItems, at the start of the bar group; without viewItems it draws none.
tucked renames, moves or hides the pin and full screen rows the main menu lists with view={false}; group and position work as in view.
A tucked label names its row in both states and activeLabel the pinned or full screen one; the bar buttons and View keep their names.
A row hidden with tucked is gone from the menu, so a narrow window that tucks its button leaves that button out of reach.
onFitChange hears which bar items a narrow window tucks away, as control:pin, control:fullscreen or action: and the action id; never read the markup for it.
Pin and full screen are menu actions whose label and icon say what a pick does; a check mark in a title bar menu means on.
a11y: Each action is an icon button named by its label, with a tooltip and aria-keyshortcuts for its shortcut.
A disabled action keeps focus with aria-disabled and describes its reason, so the keyboard reaches the tooltip; its main menu row is disabled.
A dropdown action is a menu button with aria-haspopup; its menu takes the keys of DropdownMenu.
A concealed bar opens on focus and on Alt, so the keyboard always reaches it.

tree.rule: WindowTitleBar is the one title bar of a frameless window, with the same brand, menu and controls in every app.

components.name: WorkspaceScreen
components.job: A screen to work in, built from one content object: a side nav of pages, the current page under a header that compacts as it scrolls, and a search over every setting.
useWhen: A settings hub, a profile hub or a data manager with several pages.
The user moves between pages and changes things on them.

avoidWhen.case: The screen is read and holds no settings, such as About or credits.
The screen runs one short task with a status, such as an update check.
The screen is one big surface with no pages, such as calibration.
The side nav and the page sit inside an app frame, not over it.

rules: Describe every page in content: its id, title and icon, and either sections of SettingsRow data or content of its own.
Set content.home for the Home page at the top of the nav, and content.top for more pages under it in the same block, with no heading and one divider after the block.
Every page shows the page header with its icon and title, and nothing turns it off. A screen without it is a custom screen built from ScreenWindow.
The nav, the header pills, the rows and the search all come from content; never build them by hand beside it.
Give options a hint, toggles hints for on and off and sliders hintOf, so the live hint says what each value does.
Pass activeId and onActiveChange, or search.query and search.onQueryChange, only when the host must own them.
Use the floating slot for a switch between sibling workspaces, and hidden to keep the screen mounted while it is closed.
The screen follows the room it has, not the viewport: under 640 px the side nav turns into a bar with a menu, and each page header moves its tabs under the title when they no longer fit.
a11y: The card is a modal dialog named by the title, and each page is a section named by its title.
The side nav is a navigation landmark, and every row input is named by its row title.
Escape clears a filled search before it reaches the screen.

path: working across pages, picked from a side list
tree.rule: A side list of pages beside the current page.

modules.name: marquee
modules.job: Drag a rectangle over an area to pick the items inside it, as in a file manager, with Shift to add, Ctrl or Cmd to toggle and Escape to cancel.
useWhen: An app draws a grid of tiles, files or marks and the user picks many by dragging over them.
The area scrolls and the drag must keep going when the pointer reaches its edge.

avoidWhen.case: The rectangle itself must be drawn.
The user picks rows of a table.

rules: Pass the containerRef of the box that scrolls, the selected keys and onChange; the app keeps the selection.
Spread bind on that box and draw rect with MarqueeBox inside it; rect is null when nobody drags.
Mark each item with data-marquee-key and pass its selector as itemSelector, or pass getRects with rects in the content space of the box.
A drag that starts on an item does nothing by default; pass canStart to change where a drag may start.
The drag starts after the pointer moves 4 pixels; pass threshold to change it, and enabled false to turn it off.
Shift adds to the selection, Ctrl or Cmd toggles the items inside, and Escape puts the selection back as it was.
Set touch-action none on the box when touch must drag, and pass autoScroll false to stop the scroll near its edges.
The functions rectFromPoints, rectsIntersect, hitKeys, mergeSelection and edgeScrollDelta are the same math without the hook.
a11y: Dragging is for pointers only; give the items keys or checkboxes for the same choice.
Escape cancels a drag and restores the earlier selection.
The picked items must show their own selected state, since the rectangle is hidden from readers.

modules.name: reorder
modules.job: Drag and keyboard reorder for a list or grid the app owns, as functions you wire into your own markup.
useWhen: An app builds its own reorderable list, such as a layers panel, and the rows are its own markup.
An app builds its own grid of items the user puts in order, such as a palette grid, and needs the arrow keys to move an item by a row or a column.
The same list must reorder by pointer drag and by keys, and keep focus on the moved item.

avoidWhen.case: The list is a strip of open documents with close buttons and an unsaved mark.
The list is a short set of rows the user edits in place, one input per column.

rules: Give each item data-reorder-index with its position and data-reorder-key with a stable id, as direct children of the list element, and pass the list as listRef.
Pass REORDER_ITEM_SELECTOR as the selector of useReorderDrag, and spread handlers(index) on the control the user grabs, not on the whole item.
Set axis to horizontal, vertical or grid to match the layout; onDrop gets the old and the new position and the app moves the item.
Move by keys with reorderStep: pass the key event, the axis, the chord (alt or plain), the index and the total; it returns the new position, or undefined for any other key.
When only some items are drawn, such as a windowed list, pass locate(point) to give the position from your own item model; it replaces the measure of the drawn items.
For a grid, pass columns from columnsOf(list, REORDER_ITEM_SELECTOR) so up and down move by a row.
Call expect(id) of useMoveFocus before the move so focus follows the item, and announce a sentence such as Layer moved to 3 of 8 in a live region that shows its message.
Draw the drop mark and the dragging state from dropMark(index, total) and dragging; the hook sets no style.
a11y: Keys move an item without a pointer: use the alt chord when plain arrows already move focus, and the plain chord when they do not.
The message of useMoveFocus is the announcement; render it in a polite live region, since a move changes no focus text on its own.
Focus lands on the first button of the moved item that is outside a data-reorder-toggles group, so the user keeps their place.

modules.name: virtual
modules.job: The windowing of a long list of equal rows: which rows to draw for the scroll position, and which row to keep while it holds focus.
useWhen: An app builds its own long list or table of rows of one height and draws only the rows in view.
A focused row must stay drawn when it scrolls out of view, so the keys keep working.

avoidWhen.case: A list of rows the app draws itself, with the keys already handled.
Records with columns to sort, group or resize.

rules: Pass enabled, the count of rows, keyAt that gives the stable key of a row, the rootRef of the box that scrolls and the attribute that marks a row index.
Put bodyRef on the element that holds the rows and size it to count times the row height; draw only the indices it returns.
Place each row by its index with absolute position, and mark it with the index attribute so the focus is found.
Wire onScroll to the scroll of the root, and onFocus and onBlur to the body, so a focused row stays drawn.
Keep keyAt stable with useCallback; a new function on every render measures again.
Pass sizeKey, any string that changes with the row height, so the rows are measured again; sizeVariable turns a size token name into the var() of that token.
Use scrollTopToShow to find the scroll position that brings a row into view, or scrollTopForSpan for a row of any height with an align of start, center, end or nearest.
For rows of more than one height, pass readMetrics to measure the heights and rangeOf to give the rows to draw for the scroll position; without them every row has one height.
a11y: A row that holds focus stays in the document while it is outside the window, so the keys and the screen reader keep their place.
Give each row its position and the size of the list with aria-posinset and aria-setsize, since the rest are not in the page.
